title: European-close order-flow reversal: fade a large 11:00-11:30 NY move from 12:30 to 13:55 NY, US500
ex_ante_rule: Bars: 5-minute, session-only (New York regular session 09:30-16:00); minute_of_day is local NY minutes after midnight. DAY FILTERS (all known ex ante, no price): (a) trade only when the European cash close (17:30 Europe/Berlin on that date, converted with zoneinfo) falls at 11:30 America/New_York; this skips the 2-4 weeks a year when US and European daylight-saving dates differ and Europe closes at 12:30 NY; (b) skip FOMC_today days (mark_events with kinds [FOMC]); (c) trade only on full sessions (close at 16:00 NY; half days are skipped). SIGNAL WINDOW: the 30 minutes before the European close. A = close of the bar that opens 10:55 (minute_of_day 655), B = close of the bar that opens 11:25 (minute_of_day 685, closes 11:30). R = B / A - 1. SCALE: S = mean of |R| over the previous 20 sessions that have both bars (today excluded; days skipped by filters a-c still count toward S; no trade until 20 values exist). TRIGGER: |R| >= 1.5*S and |R| >= 0.001. ENTRY: decided only at the close of the bar that opens 12:25 (minute_of_day 745), so the market order fills at the 12:30 NY bar open, 60 minutes after the European close; one decision a day, max_entries_per_day = 1. If R >= trigger (window went up): ENTER_SHORT. If R <= -trigger (window went down): ENTER_LONG. Symmetric sides. STOP on every entry: 0.4% of the 12:25-bar close, tick-rounded away from the price (long stop = tick_floor(C*0.996), short stop = tick_ceil(C*1.004)). EXIT: time exit at the close of the bar that opens 13:50 (minute_of_day 830), so the position is closed at the 13:55 bar open, before any 14:00 release; longest hold 85 minutes. Otherwise the stop. No target, no re-entry after a stop. Entry window: exactly 180 minutes after the open (210 minutes before the close). Lookbacks: 30-minute signal window, 20 sessions for S.
mechanism: Between 11:00 and 11:30 NY, European participants finish their day: European asset managers hedging or adjusting their US equity exposure, dealers in London and Frankfurt flattening the intraday S&P futures risk they took on before their desks close, and basket and cross-asset hedges tied to the 17:30 CET European close. This flow is driven by a clock and by inventory limits, not by news about US companies. It arrives just as US liquidity thins out for lunch. JPMorgan's strategists (Kolanovic et al., reported by Bloomberg on 6 July 2022) found that a large gap between buyer- and seller-initiated S&P 500 e-mini trades during the European close makes a mid-session reversal in New York more likely, and that these reversals usually start around 1 p.m. They also report that liquidity around 1 p.m. had fallen about 40% in two years, and that by 2022 less than $1bn of five-minute imbalance moved the e-mini 1% (about $6bn in 2017). On the other side are US liquidity providers who absorb the one-way flow and charge a price concession for the inventory. Once the European flow stops, they unload into the thin early afternoon and part of the concession comes back. The NY Fed's overnight-drift study documents the same inventory logic at another hand-off, the US close to the European open: an order imbalance absorbed by market makers is followed by a predictable reversal. This rule cannot see order flow, so it uses the price move in the 30-minute window as a stand-in, and trades only when that move is large against its own 20-day history.
why_gross_beats_3x_cost: On US500 the measured 30-minute median move is 9.2x the cost in the 11:00 hour, 7.7x in the 12:00 hour and 7.8x in the 13:00 hour. The 60-minute median over the whole day is 0.128% (mean 0.208%) (anatomy.json). An 85-minute midday hold therefore has a typical absolute move of about 0.12-0.18%. Trigger days have a European-close window move of at least 1.5x its 20-day average, roughly 0.15-0.3%. If the 12:30-13:55 leg gives back 15-20% of that window move on average, or equivalently the trade gets the sign right on 54-55% of trades with an average win about 1.1x the average loss, the mean gross is about 0.03-0.05% per trade, 3-5x the 0.01% round trip. The 0.4% stop is about 3x the typical midday 85-minute move, so it should fire on under 5% of trades. The 0.005% stop slippage is about 1% of the risk. The rule is short after up-windows and long after down-windows, so it does not lean on the market's upward drift. A known risk is that some large 11:00-11:30 moves are headline-driven, and those may continue.
novelty_vs_tried: P-001/P-006 (opening-range and first-candle breakouts), P-003 (noise-area breakout) and P-005 (VWAP trend) bet on continuation. So do P-002/P-004/P-007, which carry first-half-hour or rest-of-day momentum into the last half hour. All of these use the open or the whole day as reference and none trades the midday. P-008 fades the overnight-plus-first-15-minutes opening move and is flat by 10:45. P-009 trades month-end calendar flow in the last hour. The event rules traded FOMC/CPI/NFP releases. This rule's signal is a fixed 30-minute window anchored to a different market's close, the 17:30 CET European cash close, which is 11:30 NY. It ignores the open, the overnight gap and the day's trend. It enters only at 12:30 NY, after a 60-minute gap following the signal, and is flat at 13:55, so it lives entirely in the lunch session that no earlier rule touched. It skips FOMC days and the daylight-saving mismatch weeks. The counterparty is European end-of-day flow absorbed by thin US lunch liquidity, not opening imbalance, trend-following or scheduled news.
